title: Matrix Chain DP: When to Use It

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only matrix-chain program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
For dimensions [10,30,5,60], multiplying the first pair costs 1500, then multiplying its 10×5 result by 5×60 costs 3000, total 4500. The alternative parenthesization costs more; matrix order itself stays fixed.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return minimum scalar multiplications. The visible fixture is `dimensions=[10,30,5,60]` and its example result is `4500`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Matrix Chain DP when it asks for optimal parenthesisation and associative operation planning. Here the concrete task is: Return minimum scalar multiplications. The visible input `dimensions=[10,30,5,60]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Write the dependency arrows before choosing loop order; a recurrence that reads the future cannot be filled left to right without adjustment. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Try every final split of an interval and combine left cost, right cost, and multiplication cost. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A multidimensional or structured DP state records the information needed to identify a subproblem: two prefixes, an interval, a bitmask, a tree node, or a resource limit. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n^3) time · O(n^2) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `4500` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test base states, boundary cells or subsets, ties, and whether a compressed representation overwrites a value still needed later. Index tables consistently where the state is tabular. Compress dimensions only after the full recurrence and its dependency order are clear. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
